sources.title: José Clemente Orozco (Q332041), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): label 'José Clemente Orozco', description 'Mexican artist (1883-1949)', born 23 November 1883, died 7 September 1949, country Mexico, Korean label 호세 클레멘테 오로스코. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'José Clemente Orozco' (full article body read; last updated 3 September 2026). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the most important 20th-century muralist to work in fresco; he joined Rivera, Siqueiros and others in the 1923-27 National Preparatory School murals that began the Mexican muralist movement; he judged his early murals there too derivative of European traditions and destroyed many; Cortés and Malinche (1926) shows a monumentality unprecedented in Mexican art; the negative reaction to his House of Tears paintings (1917) and the withdrawal of government patronage in 1927 each sent him to the United States, where he worked to build an international reputation; Prometheus at Pomona (1930); the New School murals are faulted for a 'slavish' use of 'dynamic symmetry'; Dartmouth (1932-34) was shaped by Byzantine mosaics; he returned to Mexico in 1934 and painted Catharsis. Encyclopedic and partly critical; the superlatives are retrospective.

PBS American Masters, 'José Clemente Orozco' career timeline, read in full: night classes at the San Carlos Academy; odd jobs including architectural drafting and hand-tinting portraits; caricaturist for opposition newspapers; The House of Tears (1916) first solo show, ignored or attacked by critics; in the United States 1917-1919 painted cinema posters and dolls to earn a living; National Preparatory School murals (1923), where students defaced his work; Prometheus (1930); The Epic of American Civilization (1932-34, 24 panels); Hospicio Cabañas; Dive Bomber and Tank (1940) for the Museum of Modern Art; Supreme Court murals (1941) that drew an outcry for removal and survived; The Apocalypse (1944); Allegory of the Nation (1948), his only outdoor mural; a 1947 retrospective in Mexico. Public-television biography; the nickname 'Sistine Chapel of the Americas' is popular framing and is not used.

UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Hospicio Cabañas, Guadalajara' (Outstanding Universal Value statement, read in full): in the late 1930s the chapel was ornamented with frescoes by José Clemente Orozco, 'one of the greatest Mexican muralists of the time'; the murals are 'considered great masterpieces of Mexican art'; El Hombre de Fuego (The Man of Fire) in the dome is 'considered to be one of the masterpieces of 20th century mural painting' with profound cultural influence beyond the Americas (criterion ii); the property was inscribed for the architecture and the murals. Institutional heritage listing; retrospective praise.

U.S. National Park Service, 'The Epic of American Civilization Murals' (National Historic Landmark, designated 2013), read in full: Orozco was a visiting lecturer in the Dartmouth art department in May 1932; the 24 true-fresco panels (about 3,200 square feet) cover four walls of the Baker Library reserve reading room, painted 1932-34; the theme responded to the Mexican Civil War and World War I and to nationalism and industrialisation; placement in a college founded to educate Native Americans was intentional; Orozco with Rivera and Siqueiros helped introduce Mexican mural art to the United States and so helped inspire the New Deal mural movement. Federal heritage page; does not discuss controversy.

Dartmouth Alumni Magazine, 'History of the Project' (November 1933, by the chairman of the college art department), read in full: Dartmouth commissioned Orozco in June 1932 for a fresco in the Baker Library reserve room; a small 'Release' panel was first painted to demonstrate true fresco; while painting it he proposed an 'Epic of Civilization on the American Continent'; the trustees approved it on educational grounds; he was made visiting professor of art, taught 'by doing' with the reading room as his lecture hall, worked almost entirely alone apart from a plasterer, and the job took about two years with about half spent painting. Contemporary, but written by the department that hired him, so promotional and admiring; no criticism appears in it.

Dartmouth course website (SPAN 7, Winter 2017), student post 'Authorization of the Orozco Murals', read in full: professors Packard and Lathrop invited Orozco with President Hopkins' support; a Rockefeller family fund paid for the project; alumni, including a telephone-company president in a letter of 3 June 1932, objected that a college gives official approval to art on its walls; some viewers disliked the panels on education and Christ; the criticism came close to the fresco being painted over but the college kept the murals open. A student course blog quoting archived records; used only as the counter-voice for the controversy, not for any claim about Orozco's own response, which it does not record.

TIME magazine, 'Art: Wall Man' (13 October 1930), read in full: Orozco painted a fresco about 25 by 35 feet of Prometheus in the Pomona College dining hall; true fresco worked in sections of about two square yards beside a master plasterer, each day's section begun at the same hour because fresco 'has much to do with the time of day'; at the New School for Social Research he worked from a scaffold with a small brush; when Pomona could offer only $500 he reportedly asked 'Have you got a wall?'; the Los Angeles Times critic Arthur Millier and the Denver Times critic Arnold Ronnebeck praised the Pomona wall. Contemporary independent press; the quotation is a reported anecdote.

Museum of Modern Art press release and press-conference invitation, 17-18 June 1940 (MoMA press archives PDF), read in full: the museum commissioned Orozco to paint a fresco, 'The Dive Bomber', on its gallery wall as part of Twenty Centuries of Mexican Art; true fresco on six plaster panels attached to the wall so that it could later be shown elsewhere; visitors could watch each afternoon; Orozco said the panels could be turned or rearranged in any order and that a picture must be capable of being looked at from any direction; asked about political meaning he said none was intended and that each viewer can draw their own meaning; he expected the work to take about four weeks. Institutional publicity, partly in Orozco's own reported words; it states he had no formal art training, which Britannica contradicts (Academy of San Carlos), so that line is not used.

Pomona College Museum of Art, exhibition page on Orozco's 'Prometheus' (Frary Dining Hall), read in full: Orozco chose the Greek myth of Prometheus as suited to the college; the central panel is credited to Orozco and the flanking panels to Orozco and Jorge Juan Crespo de la Serna; the page marks the mural's 80th anniversary and preservation efforts and says few current students know its history. College museum page; thin on technique and reception.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_unesco, src_orozco_nps, src_orozco_time1930 | 1923-1934 | encyclopedia + heritage body + federal landmark page + contemporary press] Britannica says he judged his early Preparatory School murals too derivative of European traditions and destroyed many, and that Cortés and Malinche (1926) shows a monumentality unprecedented in Mexican art; it is not uniformly admiring, since it faults the New School murals for a 'slavish' use of dynamic symmetry. UNESCO calls the Man of Fire dome one of the masterpieces of 20th-century mural painting, the National Park Service calls the Dartmouth cycle a seminal work, and a 1930 critic praised the Pomona wall. Most of the praise is retrospective and institutional, so confidence stays moderate.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_pbs | 1927-1947 | encyclopedia + public-television biography] Britannica says that after settling in New York he consciously strove to build an international reputation that would force his countrymen to recognise his value, and PBS lists the sequence of United States commissions, a Colegio de México fellowship and the 1947 retrospective in Mexico. The motive rests on one encyclopedia sentence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a high-risk row; lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.45 because the stated motive rests on a single source and no independent account confirms it.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_orozco_britannica | 1923-1926 | encyclopedia] Britannica says he was dissatisfied with his early National Preparatory School murals, judged them too derivative of European traditions and destroyed many of them before the 1926 panels in which he came into his own style. That shows a high standard applied to his own finished work; it is one source and does not show a general habit of over-refinement, so the row is modest.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_time1930, src_orozco_dartmag | 1905-1934 | encyclopedia + contemporary press + department chair's account] Britannica says he re-entered the Academy of San Carlos in 1905 and set about becoming a competent painter, and that a 1932 European trip, including Byzantine mosaics, shaped the Dartmouth cycle. TIME (1930) describes true fresco worked in small sections beside a plasterer, begun at a fixed hour each day for even drying, and the 1933 Dartmouth account says he first painted a small demonstration panel in true fresco. The Dartmouth account is promotional, so it is corroboration only.

persistence.rationale: [src_orozco_pbs, src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_nps, src_orozco_dartmag | 1917-1934 | public-television biography + encyclopedia + federal page + department chair's account] PBS records that his first solo show was ignored or attacked, that he earned a living in the United States in 1917-1919 with cinema posters and dolls, and that students defaced his Preparatory School work; Britannica says that after patronage was withdrawn in 1927 he went again to the United States and returned to Mexico in 1934. The NPS gives the Dartmouth cycle as 24 true-fresco panels painted 1932-34, and the 1933 account says he worked almost entirely alone with a plasterer for about two years. The last point comes from an admiring source and the 'persistence' is partly inferred from the scale of the work.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_orozco_pbs, src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_dartblog | 1917-1941 | public-television biography + encyclopedia + student course post] PBS says critics ignored or attacked his 1916 exhibition and that his Supreme Court murals drew calls for removal but survived; the course post records alumni objections at Dartmouth that nearly led to the fresco being painted over. Britannica says negative critical reaction in 1917 and the attacks after 1927 each led him to leave Mexico for the United States. The sources show that he kept producing critical, controversial work, but they do not record how he responded in the disputes, and the survival of the Dartmouth and Supreme Court murals was decided by others. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a high-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.55 to 60 / 0.45 because the trait claim was stronger than the documented behaviour (he left Mexico twice after attacks, and no source records his own stance in the disputes).

adaptability.rationale: [src_orozco_pbs, src_orozco_britannica, src_orozco_moma1940 | 1904-1940 | public-television biography + encyclopedia + museum press release] He moved from caricature for opposition newspapers to fresco, worked in the United States in very different jobs and settings, and by 1940 painted a fresco in six movable panels in a New York museum gallery while visitors watched, saying the panels could be rearranged in any order. Britannica adds that he turned in Prometheus to a universal theme and a Michelangelo-influenced style. The evidence shows movement between formats, places and styles but little on how he coped with change itself.

portrait.source: Los Angeles Times photograph of Orozco on his arrival at a Los Angeles train station, 20 March 1930, published with a Los Angeles Times article of 21 March 1930 (page A9); glass negative in the Los Angeles Times Photographic Archive, UCLA Library Special Collections (identifier uclamss_1429_b3720_G3540). The file is the original 3774 x 4375 scan downscaled to 1035 x 1200 with no cropping and no upscaling.

portrait.attribution: Photo: Los Angeles Times, 20 March 1930; Los Angeles Times Photographic Archive, UCLA Library Special Collections (via Wikimedia Commons)
portrait.creator: Los Angeles Times (staff photographer, not named)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / FOUND, same photograph as the lead (Los Angeles Times, 20-21 March 1930, UCLA Library). The UCLA record page itself is behind a bot-wall (Anubis proof-of-work) and was not bypassed; the Calisphere item page for the same ark (opened) gives the holder's metadata instead: date 20 March 1930, 'Photo (cropped) appears with the article PAINTER TO PUT MURALS IN COLLEGE ... Los Angeles Times, 21 Mar. 1930: A9', identifier uclamss_1429_b3720_G3540, glass negative, and a 'rights information' line that is only UCLA Special Collections contact details (no Creative Commons wording at item level). The Commons file page (opened) carries the collection-level 'LATimes UCLA' CC BY 4.0 tag saying only that 'the bulk' of the digitised images are under CC BY 4.0, with no item-level licence line, and I found secondhand mention that older UCLA pages once carried a non-commercial licence, so the CC tag alone is NOT relied on. RIGHTS BASIS USED: age. The holder's own record dates the photograph to 20 March 1930 and states it was published in the Los Angeles Times on 21 March 1930, a work published in the United States before 1931 whose 95-year term ended on 31 December 2025, so it is in the US public domain as of 1 January 2026; UCLA also holds the copyright (deeded by the newspaper) and offers the scan under CC BY 4.0, so both bases point the same way and credit is given. Caveat for the lead: the age basis depends on the holder's statement that this exact image was published in 1930; the Commons image is the uncropped negative scan and the published version was cropped. Original 3774 x 4375 downloaded and confirmed; downscaled to 1035 x 1200 (no upscaling, no cropping); sitter identified by the holder's caption and the negative-sleeve text 'Orozco, Jose C. Artist. 1930'. kind likeness. EXCLUSIONS: the 'Sistine Chapel of the Americas' nickname (tourism framing), claims that Prometheus was the first fresco in the United States (attributed to one page and disputed by wording), the dates and circumstances of his hand injury (sources conflict between 17 and 21 and it is not scored), political ideology comparisons with Rivera and Siqueiros (unsourced in the article that makes them), and the Revolution-era partisan work. Date conflicts recorded: the United States trip is dated 1916-17 by some sources and 1917 by Britannica and PBS; MoMA's release says he had no formal art training while Britannica and PBS record Academy of San Carlos study.
